comments.comment_body_raw:
> but in general, the fact that documents open and close differently depending on how they were opened seems incorrect.

It is not intuitive but it is correct and something that will not change. Extensions can only open text documents, we don't allow extensions to close documents. Because that again would imply a contract in which we need to keep a document open and the renderer's memory consumption would be at the mercy of extensions hopefully calling close. 

> Is there a way to trigger diagnostics refresh/updates for a document, from EH?

There is no such way because even VS Code doesn't know when diagnostics come in. They just happen and VS Code shows them.

@jrieken 
> even VS Code doesn't know when diagnostics come in. They just happen and VS Code shows them.

Okay, can it be then, that it is a question about closing editors, not documents? There is some events happen when editor of a document which was opened from Explorer, closed, and these events doesn't fired on editor close of a document opened from EH.

These events are (immediately after editor is closed):
c) Diagnostic entries of a document of that editor are removed from marker service `language` collection
d) Marker service `mirrorCollection`, which is a storage of diagnostic entries of tasks problem matchers, gets repopulated
So, these events happen on normal tab close, and does not happen on tab close of `openTextDocument` opened files

But. There is also events which happen on editor open, which are:
a) `mirrorCollection` gets updated by empty list of diagnostics, by call of [ExtHostDiagnostics.$acceptMarkersChange](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/blob/1709b5eb569626abd6f7136894de81efa2b1c562/src/vs/workbench/api/common/extHostDiagnostics.ts#L351) which is needed to work with only problems reported by language extension, while editor is open
b) Marker service `language` collection is updated by adding diagnostics coming from language extension
And this happens no matter of the method of document opening

What is responsible for calling these events? It looks like it handles editors opening of both ways, but doesn't handle editor closing of the `openTextDocument` use. Like, some callbacks subscriptions for editor close events are missing in the case of using it

I mean, if something already takes care of a) and b) for both methods, it should also take care of c) and d), for both ways, since they are paired, on editor open giagnostics removed from `mirrorCollection` and added to `language` collection. On editor close events do the reverse. If something execute one part, it should execute second. Since it doesn't, it is a bug

@jrieken @RedCMD I found that it is related to `typescript-language-features` extension work
It subscribes to documents open and close as
https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/blob/88dc2db2e856def99447180fb2fbdf3fda621a7b/extensions/typescript-language-features/src/tsServer/bufferSyncSupport.ts#L531-L532
And it updates diagnostics based on these events

The problem is that `onDidCloseTextDocument` is not fired immediately if it was open by `vscode.workspace.openTextDocument()`. Though it is fired 3 min later and diagnostics removed from Problems View, something already happens in ts server by that time, and it doesn't replace diagnostics by tsc problem matcher outputs.
For test, I have set auto dispose timer to `-1` at https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/blob/88dc2db2e856def99447180fb2fbdf3fda621a7b/src/vs/workbench/api/browser/mainThreadDocuments.ts#L35

This made the trick, diagnostics gets replaced immediately. But even a small delay of 1 ms sometimes leads to the loss of task outputs lists

Now the question is, do we still agree that deviations of documents opening from Explorer (and maybe from somewhere else) and from EH by `vscode.workspace.openTextDocument()` are considered normal? Since this shows that not all scenarios can be relied upon `vscode.workspace.onDidCloseTextDocument` and maybe ts server is not the only place which has issues with this.
If yes, how it should be fixed? Should ts server switch from using `vscode.workspace.onDidOpen/Close` to events related to visibleEditors or tabs/tabGroups? Do I need to create new issue, or I can try to implement a fix in PR? Or someone from Team take it? I would like to help and speed it up, if I can

I discovered that the diagnostics are not repushed to markerService due to the incorrect uri comparison by reference here
https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/blob/e6f0ffde9cd540816b4a1b22e7520424cfa58fdd/src/vs/workbench/contrib/tasks/common/problemCollectors.ts#L451
For documents opened from explorer it works, but when `vscode.workspace.openTextDocument` is used, `!markerEvent.includes(modelEvent.uri)` fails. Fixing it to compare by `Uri.toString()` makes problem matcher output correctly repushed on document disposal after 3 min delay. Now we should not lose the tracking of problems when using `vscode.workspace.openTextDocument` at least

Okay, now I'm personally fine with that markerService  keeps holding diagnostics from extension for 3 min after closing a file which was opened by `vscode.workspace.openTextDocument`. But it feels wrong, the possibility to update diagnostics on demand should exist. Or it is there, and I just don't see it? https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/blob/e6f0ffde9cd540816b4a1b22e7520424cfa58fdd/src/vs/workbench/contrib/tasks/common/problemCollectors.ts#L443

> that markerService keeps holding diagnostics from extension for 3 min after closing a file which was opened by vscode.workspace.openTextDocument. But it feels wrong, the possibility to update diagnostics on demand should exist. 

Again, it is up to extensions. The problem is that in the beginning we only had `onDid[Open|Close]TextDocument` events and that the `tabGroups` API came later and therefore many extensions keep diagnostics around for too long. Tho, it is arguable what "too long" means. There is two types

1) Problem exists because of a project configuration (like tsconfig.json) and those shouldn't disappear just because the editor or document closes. These are problems that will also fail your CI
2) Then there is also "editor-only" problems, like spelling markers, and those aren't (most likely) not interesting after closing the editor anymore

comments.comment_body_raw:
@jrieken 
> Again, it is up to extensions. The problem is that in the beginning we only had `onDid[Open|Close]TextDocument` events and that the `tabGroups` API came later and therefore many extensions keep diagnostics around for too long. Tho, it is arguable what "too long" means. There is two types

Unfortunately, it is not only up to extensions. If we switch to `tabGroups` API, what happens is - extension clears diagnostics on editor removal, but in case of problem matcher running we get a time gap of up to 3 mins, during which there is no diagnostics info in markerService, since problem matcher is not aware about the need of updating it, and does it on textModel dispose only. This may never happen at all probably, if something else will keep holding textModel alive:
https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/blob/a5914335df0bf1cae7d818a168ef321def9f8572/src/vs/workbench/contrib/tasks/common/problemCollectors.ts#L443

So, to make it work properly and unstick from document instantiation and disposing, just switching extensions to the usage of `tabGroups` events is not enough.

I would leave it as is after accepted repushing fix. But I managed to gain a more comprehensive understanding of the processes taking place while I was sorting out these issues, and now I can’t leave this without my proposal =)
Please take the time to review it when possible, as the changes may be more substantial than it appears from my view, and I may have overlooked some caveats


###### suggestion
Let me describe current situation briefly. We have marker providers which push their markers to markerService. Markers land in 2-d storage divided by `owner`, which is a language sign, and `resource`, which is uri (or its path). This is fine until we get into situation when more that one marker provider manages markers of the same owner+resource, such as in `typescript-language-features` extension and `tsc problem-matcher`. This makes a collision, where one may overwrite each other markers inside markerService, and as it seems to me, it is the main reason of making [WatchingProblemCollector](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/blob/a5914335df0bf1cae7d818a168ef321def9f8572/src/vs/workbench/contrib/tasks/common/problemCollectors.ts#L412) to repush markers on textModel dispose, and also along with [StartStopProblemCollector](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/blob/a5914335df0bf1cae7d818a168ef321def9f8572/src/vs/workbench/contrib/tasks/common/problemCollectors.ts#L359) to filter their pushes by the textModel opened/closed status, like here [if (shouldApplyMatch)](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/blob/a5914335df0bf1cae7d818a168ef321def9f8572/src/vs/workbench/contrib/tasks/common/problemCollectors.ts#L392). So, problem matchers filter their outputs based on the **assumption** that there may be other marker provider active, to not mess with it. This mechanic is not bulletproof and may create more issues in the future if more marker providers appear, and this already creates issue in the scenario discussed there. So this is the first thing we change - we let marker providers push their data to markerService without collision preventing workarounds, by adding a `origin` tag in addition to `owner` and `resource`. `origin` entity is already added by @dbaeumer https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/issues/251268#issuecomment-3024704155, https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/pull/253368, and now we can take it to the more substantive usage with some adjustments. For now, `origin` is `string | undefined` and is set as string for the markers originated from extension host, and undefined for everything else.

So, the first is - we removing repushes of markers by `WatchingProblemCollector` on textModel dispose, and remove their outputs filtering based on textModel existence. Simply push any marker updates to `markerService`. This significantly simplifies the update logic for marker providers

Now, the essence of suggestion is `markerService` improvement to make it able to switch active origin (naming is under the question, it may be named `visible/presenting/facadeOrigin`,  but for now I just called it `activeOrigin`), which means that [MarkerService.read](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/blob/a5914335df0bf1cae7d818a168ef321def9f8572/src/vs/platform/markers/common/markerService.ts#L332) called for `owner` and `resource` outputs only markers for active origin, and triggers [onMarkerChanged](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/blob/a5914335df0bf1cae7d818a168ef321def9f8572/src/vs/platform/markers/common/markerService.ts#L158) event for updates of active origin markers only. Updates of other origins for the given owner+resource are still served, but they land to '`backyard`' storage, not visible in output and don't fire onMarkerChanged events

Thats it, it s actually simple idea. I may be unaware of impossibility of this change, but at a first glance, I like how it works. What do we get if we implement it:
1. Marker providers update pushes simplification
2. Markers storage is always up to date
3. Active origin switch is instant
4. Origin can be turned into more complex object with a hierarchy structure in the future, which may include origins prioritization logics. For example, for now we have only two priority levels - problem matchers (and maybe something else), for which we can leave origin as undefined for now, and a extension diagnostics level, which is more prioritized. There could be more levels between these two in the future, lets say we have a problem matcher diagnostics as a lowest one, then if there is some language service pushes markers it may have higher priority, and a language extension even more prioritized when a document is presented for editing. When document is removed from ui, markerService switch activeOrigin to another, language service in this case. If language service disappears, it switches to undefined origin, which is problem matchers atm. Probably too many words used to explain simple prioritization mechanics =)

Let me demonstrate it in action, so that you don't need to test it yourself right now. Pay attension to Problems View panel's `another.ts` diagnostics. The last problem of it is treated as Error by tsc watcher, and treated as Warning by typescript extension. So the orange/red icon serves as an indicator of who the diagnostic source is, at the moment. I just open and close files from explorer, and also by calling a command of test extension, which simply opens another.ts by hardcoded path, for testing

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/be3c2691-a2d5-420e-b15a-797e29df043b)

You can check changes in PR to my vscode fork if need: https://github.com/n-gist/vscode/pull/1
There is a lot of files touched by changes in typescript extension and problem matcher applyTo attribute removal, so I have combined essential changes in third commit https://github.com/n-gist/vscode/pull/1/changes/7bcaf10fe9327d1862c5906791f8b4f0e64725ab
This is a prototype, made to just prove (myself) that this can be done. I have left some comments in edits

IAccording to my plan, the finished version will include:
1. Removing `origin` property from [IMarker](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/blob/a5914335df0bf1cae7d818a168ef321def9f8572/src/vs/platform/markers/common/markers.ts#L129) (and [IMarkerData](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/blob/a5914335df0bf1cae7d818a168ef321def9f8572/src/vs/platform/markers/common/markers.ts#L109)) objects
2. Passing `origin` as argument to `MarkerService` `remove`, `changeOne`, `installResourceFilter`?, and adding it to IResourceMarker to support `changeAll`
3. We can add explicit methods for claiming/releasing the activity for an origin, but for now, just automatic switch seems sufficient. For now it simply proclaims and origin as active when it receives any markers which has it, and releases activity when it gets `null`. This is not stable at the moment due to the lack of `origin`, but after adding it as argument and checking all callers, this should be good. In this case we declare, that `null` passed as `markerData` clears markers for the origin, and releases it from being active, if it is, and switches activity to another one, by prioritization rules
4. Removal of `applyTo` property for problem matches may be an overmuch. But it is set as `allDocuments` for the most, and only in some cases it is set to `closeDocuments` for some tsc tasks only, which we probably cover by this change. This can be kept if there is another reasons for having it

If anyone wants to test it on the same project I have used in video, `git clone git@github.com:n-gist/getDiagnostics-test.git`, `npm install` for tsc if need. `diag-vanish-tester-1.0.0.vsix` is the extension to test opening another.ts from EH by `Vanish Tester: Open` command

So, if this idea is viable, I could complete the points of my plan and make a PR. Though I may have additional questions, and let me know if there are issues out of my view I need to take care of

comments.comment_body_raw:
/cc @pohly 
Not sure what of this we need versus the test driver we use extensively today, thoughts?

----

For device-plugin, we never had a good mock driver AIUI. 

So we kinda needed to test with the real hardware setup we had, and it didn't make sense to kick out the working tests while investment was going to DRA. 

So we (mostly @dims) patched that up and made sure we still had some actual coverage for this, especially while that type of workload was booming and DRA was not GA yet ...

If we're actively investing in new things, I'm less sure about putting more vendor bits in k/k, but I don't think we say _never_, we've had cri-o (sometimes even in prod kubelet code!) and containerd bits here for example. We have to weigh the tradeoffs and make sure we can achieve good test coverage for Kubernetes.

> [AMD DRA Driver](https://github.com/ROCm/k8s-gpu-dra-driver) does exist and I'm not saying that we should add this into our CI right now. I just want to understand what would be the process for other device vendors if we want one.

The first problem would be an environment to test in, we have substantial credits and test tooling on GCP and AWS in particular where we can bring up k8s from source. Those clouds have NVIDIA GPUs and we have tooling that works with this (including sigs.k8s.io/boskos and the cluster tools), but I don't think AMD GPUs are even available at all in the public clouds.

If they became available there, we could revisit.

Similarly we could revisit if we got credits for a neocloud or something, but it's quite a lot of additional work to ensure Kubernetes *at HEAD* works in an environment, most production tooling is going to lag our releases and often repackage them a bit, so the requirement to be continuously supported at HEAD blocks out e.g. https://github.com/kubernetes/k8s.io/issues/8946 from readily working and I doubt we'd be doing this anytime soon.

I think if they did though, we'd strongly consider making these tests work with that driver as well.

But this is why we never did for device-plugin for example ... no supportable test environment with that hardware.

comments.comment_body_raw:
I think we *shouldn't* do this.

Testing with one specific vendor driver and hardware is not going to provide additional code coverage beyond what we already have with the in-tree test driver. For simulating "real" vendor hardware we plan to add "profiles" to the out-of-tree example driver which then more faithfully emulate the number of devices and their attributes of specific hardware.

That leaves integration-style testing *of the vendor's software stack* as justification. Isn't that something that a vendor should be doing? We intentionally publish alpha and release candidates and have a long code freeze period. Vendors can and should use that to make sure that the upcoming Kubernetes release works for them (regarding new features) and doesn't regress. Picking one vendor and doing that work for them won't scale.

comments.comment_body_raw:
Hey folks, SIG Testing has actually been working to minimize the set of e2e images, I think we need to update some docs to surface this better.

There is a linter that requires a racheting allowlist of images when used in the tests, but I guess nothing to catch a new `test/images/.*` folder and the docs in the test/images root still discuss how you would add a new imge.

Keeping these patched is problematic, this probably should be made a subcommand of test/images/agnhost instead of a new image. Can we please investigate this approach while we work to update the docs etc?

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/a841d1142058555c2e55c591a22e8fa31cdea88e/test/images/.permitted-images#L1-L9

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/131893

comments.comment_body_raw:
Hi @ndixita 

I’m currently working on the implementation for pod-level resource limits defaulting, based on the guidance that pod-level limits should be derived from aggregated container limits **only when**:

1. Pod-level resource requests are explicitly set, and
2. All containers in the pod have resource limits set.

I’d like to clarify an edge case around what it means for *“all containers to have limits set”*.

Consider a pod with three containers:

* Container A sets a CPU limit but does **not** set a memory limit
* Container B sets a memory limit but does **not** set a CPU limit
* Container C sets both CPU and memory limits

In this situation, each resource dimension (CPU, memory) is covered by at least one container, but **no single container defines limits for all resources**.

My questions are:

* Should this pod be treated as *not having all container limits set*, and therefore **skip defaulting pod-level limits and return early**?
* Or should defaulting be evaluated **per resource dimension**, meaning we aggregate CPU limits from containers that define CPU limits and memory limits from containers that define memory limits?
* If the latter is intended, how should we treat containers that omit a specific resource limit — should they be assumed unbounded for that resource, or excluded from the aggregation?

I want to ensure the implementation aligns with the intent behind avoiding pods having access to “unknown” resources while still handling partial container specifications consistently.

Any clarification or pointers to prior discussions would be very helpful.
Thank you for your time and guidance.

comments.comment_body_raw:
Looking at nginx Ingress, here is the information gather by my 'agent'...

Short answer: the controller does not special‑case, normalize, or reject IP addresses in the Ingress rule hosts. It passes the string through and renders it into NGINX’s server_name as-is. That has different outcomes for IPv4 vs IPv6.

What happens in code
- Host is taken verbatim into the Server object
  - controller.createServers(): rule.Host is copied into server.Hostname (empty -> "_") with no IP/DNS validation
    - file: internal/ingress/controller/controller.go
- The NGINX template renders server_name using that hostname unchanged (except for wildcard handling)
  - template: server_name {{ buildServerName $server.Hostname }} …
    - file: rootfs/etc/nginx/template/nginx.tmpl
  - buildServerName only rewrites wildcard names; otherwise returns the input string
    - file: internal/ingress/controller/template/template.go (buildServerName)
- Admission/safety checks do not reject IP hosts
  - inspector.CheckRegex() only blocks dangerous substrings (alias/root/etc); it does not validate DNS vs IP
    - file: internal/ingress/inspector/{ingress.go,rules.go}
- TLS certificate selection for such a host will use the host string
  - verifyHostname() treats IPs specially and only matches against IP SANs
    - file: internal/ingress/controller/certificate.go (verifyHostname)

Resulting behavior
- IPv4 host (e.g., 203.0.113.10)
  - NGINX gets: server_name 203.0.113.10; This is valid in NGINX and will match requests whose Host header is that IP.
  - TLS: the controller will associate a cert only if it has the IP in its SANs; otherwise it falls back to the default cert. Note many clients don’t send SNI for IP literals, so the default cert may be served at handshake time regardless.
- IPv6 host (e.g., 2001:db8::1)
  - NGINX would be rendered with: server_name 2001:db8::1; Colons aren’t valid in server_name tokens. On reload, the controller runs nginx -t (testTemplate in internal/ingress/controller/nginx.go); nginx -t will fail, so the reload is aborted and the previous (last good) config stays active.

Bottom line

Looking at nginx Ingress, here is the information gather by my 'agent'...

Short answer: the controller does not special‑case, normalize, or reject IP addresses in the Ingress rule hosts. It passes the string through and renders it into NGINX’s server_name as-is. That has different outcomes for IPv4 vs IPv6.

What happens in code
- Host is taken verbatim into the Server object
  - controller.createServers(): rule.Host is copied into server.Hostname (empty -> "_") with no IP/DNS validation
    - file: internal/ingress/controller/controller.go
- The NGINX template renders server_name using that hostname unchanged (except for wildcard handling)
  - template: server_name {{ buildServerName $server.Hostname }} …
    - file: rootfs/etc/nginx/template/nginx.tmpl
  - buildServerName only rewrites wildcard names; otherwise returns the input string
    - file: internal/ingress/controller/template/template.go (buildServerName)
- Admission/safety checks do not reject IP hosts
  - inspector.CheckRegex() only blocks dangerous substrings (alias/root/etc); it does not validate DNS vs IP
    - file: internal/ingress/inspector/{ingress.go,rules.go}
- TLS certificate selection for such a host will use the host string
  - verifyHostname() treats IPs specially and only matches against IP SANs
    - file: internal/ingress/controller/certificate.go (verifyHostname)

Resulting behavior
- IPv4 host (e.g., 203.0.113.10)
  - NGINX gets: server_name 203.0.113.10; This is valid in NGINX and will match requests whose Host header is that IP.
  - TLS: the controller will associate a cert only if it has the IP in its SANs; otherwise it falls back to the default cert. Note many clients don’t send SNI for IP literals, so the default cert may be served at handshake time regardless.
- IPv6 host (e.g., 2001:db8::1)
  - NGINX would be rendered with: server_name 2001:db8::1; Colons aren’t valid in server_name tokens. On reload, the controller runs nginx -t (testTemplate in internal/ingress/controller/nginx.go); nginx -t will fail, so the reload is aborted and the previous (last good) config stays active.

Bottom line
- The controller accepts and forwards IP hosts unchanged.
- IPv4 literal hosts work (host-based vhost keyed to the IP in the Host header); TLS requires an IP SAN to avoid cert mismatch. 
- IPv6 literal hosts cause an invalid NGINX configuration and prevent reload.

comments.comment_body_raw:
Here is the info about the Gateway behavior: in short, the IP V4 would get through, but is not supposed to be supported.
I will test behavior with Envoy Gateway provider as a started and see what happens, but Gateway may also need some formal modification to support this fully.

> Short answer:
> - Not supported. Gateway API Hostname fields explicitly disallow IP literals. That applies to both IPv4 and IPv6.
> - IPv6 literals will be rejected by schema validation (fail fast at admission) because the Hostname regex only allows DNS labels (no colons/brackets).
> - IPv4 literals are also disallowed by spec; however, the regex used for Hostname matches RFC1123 labels and can accept something that looks like 10.0.0.1. Although such values may be admitted by the API server, they are non-conformant and behavior is implementation-specific. Do not rely on them.
> 
> What the code and CRDs say:
> - apis/v1/shared_types.go: Hostname string
>   • Comment: “IPs are not allowed.”
>   • Validation: Pattern ^(\*\.)?[a-z0-9]([-a-z0-9]*[a-z0-9])?(\.[a-z0-9]([-a-z0-9]*[a-z0-9])?)*$
> - apis/v1/httproute_types.go (and grpc/tls routes): Hostname/hostnames fields repeat “IPs are not allowed.”
> - Listener.hostname is also Hostname (same regex and rule; config/crd/.../gateways.yaml has XValidations using the same pattern). 
> - TLSRoute SNI hostnames: CRD descriptions explicitly state “IPs are not allowed in SNI names per RFC 6066.”
> - PreciseHostname (used e.g., for HTTPRequestRedirect.hostname and some response rewriting): comment says numeric IP addresses are not allowed with its own pattern.
> 
> Expected behavior by case:
> - HTTPRoute.spec.hostnames or GRPCRoute.spec.hostnames set to an IPv6 literal (e.g., [2001:db8::1], or 2001:db8::1): rejected at admission with a pattern-validation error. This is a graceful, early failure.
> - Listener.hostname set to IPv6 literal: same, rejected at admission.
> - Any field typed as PreciseHostname set to IP (v4 or v6): rejected at admission.
> - HTTPRoute/GRPCRoute hostnames set to IPv4 literal (e.g., 10.0.0.1): spec says “IPs are not allowed”, but the regex can admit this because RFC1123 permits numeric labels. If admitted, it’s non-conformant; controllers are not required to support it. Possible outcomes are implementation-specific: some may ignore/mismatch; others may match literally; status conditions like NoMatchingListenerHostname could appear depending on the controller’s handling. There is no guarantee.
> 
> Guidance and workarounds:
> - Don’t use IPs in Hostname/hostnames anywhere in Gateway API routing rules. Use DNS names.
> - If you need to accept requests addressed to the Gateway IP (client sends Host: 10.0.0.1), leave Listener.hostname and Route hostnames unset so they match all hostnames; route by path/headers instead. You cannot explicitly match the IP literal via hostnames in a conformant way.
> - For fields that describe external origins/URIs (e.g., CORSOrigin, AbsoluteURI), IP hosts are allowed, but those are not used for hostname routing intersection; they are separate features.
> 
> Bottom line:
> - IPv4 and IPv6 IPs are not supported as Gateway routing hostnames. IPv6 is always rejected by schema; IPv4 may pass schema but is still out-of-spec and behavior is controller-dependent. Prefer DNS names or leave hostnames empty to match all.

comments.comment_body_raw:
Hmm, this still shows at least a concurrency issue in our tests that could be triggered. I think that warrants a fix at minimum. 

> Without this artificial delay, the initialization completes before any other code can interact with the locks.

Are we sure about this? While it seems unlikely that this can happen, I looked through the traces and spotted some concerning sections with the sleep that @user12031 showed.

The run lock is trying to be acquired by the `run` function and the distribute function is being called by `processReplacedListInfo` in `controller.go`. This does seem like it can happen in a real scenario, however unlikely it is.

```
	defer wg.Wait()                                         // Wait for Processor to stop
	defer stopProcessor(errors.New("informer is stopping")) // Tell Processor to stop
	// TODO: extend the MutationDetector interface so that it optionally
	// has a RunWithContext method that we can use here.
	wg.StartWithChannel(processorStopCtx.Done(), s.cacheMutationDetector.Run)
	wg.StartWithContext(processorStopCtx, s.processor.run)

	defer func() {
		s.startedLock.Lock()
		defer s.startedLock.Unlock()
		s.stopped = true // Don't want any new listeners
	}()
	s.controller.RunWithContext(ctx)
```

Due to the fact that wg.Wait only pauses after `s.controller.RunWithContext(ctx)` starts up is a bit of a concern. This seems like the root cause of the issue, since the controller will eventually trigger a replace which adds elements to the informer before it is started, strange...

Since this hasn't been reported on a live env, it seems likely that the informer starts up far quicker than the controller starts pushing events, but I agree that this looks like a real deadlock, possibly worse than just a goroutine leak. I think the main reason we don't see this is that the controller starting a watch is a far greater magnitude of time than the startup time of an informer.

cc @liggitt @pohly

comments.comment_body_raw:
some musings:
first and foremost, this small enhancement seems reasonnable and useful to me. I agree it would be good to have it.

next, I'd also prefer kubelet to set the values because the current model is kubelet owning the node and the cgroup management of pods (with everything else built upon that).
I'm advocating since quite some time to start thinking about how the kubelet can delegate these responsabilities to other components, like a [CPU DRA driver](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/dra-driver-cpu), so why prefer kubelet owning this setting? Because I think the best path is for the community to agree and design a proper delegation model rather than go piecewise following specific issues, because this creates a fragmented space harder to integrate later on and an explosion of special conditions, which we have plenty already. The path should be _conceptually_ like docker -> CRI we did in the quite distant past (and we can totally start with a small well defined core and iterate later on).

So, kubelet should own it only if the kernel supports it, which seems fair so far. Next question would be if use should control it or not (e.g. emergency disable). I think defaulting to this behavior seems the most user-friendly choice and an emergency disable FG seems the best approach.

Which made me think if this work deserves a small KEP because we're actually doing all the things the KEP process mandates, but informally here: thinking about integration parts, impacts on the ecosystem, UX flow, failure modes...

comments.comment_body_raw:
> 我希望 kubelet 被告知应该设置什么值，并在知道该设置值时进行设置。我想，如果 cpu.shares 已经设置好了，kubelet 也可以学习不再尝试设置它。
> 
> 我想，在颠覆性测试套件中，我们可以调度一个非常消耗 CPU 资源的保证型 Pod，它会执行大量 CPU 操作，然后写入一个文件；然后再调度一个尽力而为型 Pod，如果该文件没有写入成功，则该 Pod 会失败。如果在保证型 Pod 运行期间，允许尽力而为型 Pod 获取 CPU 时间，那么它就会失败。不过，这种方法可能不太稳定，而且我猜想它可能会捕获 CI 中一些奇怪的内核 bug。

if enable cpu.idle , the same level directory cpu.shares values will be set to 3 this is kernel action https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/v6.18/kernel/sched/fair.c#L13592
in original kubelet code , besteffort  level cpu.shares will be set to 2 , this is min value of cpu.shares
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/028015267e30a5f4f975c9a57f91f53ddd79eca5/pkg/kubelet/cm/qos_container_manager_linux.go#L106
hope this information is helpful to you

This approach would involve minimal and simplest changes, and there would be no need to worry about potential side effects from introducing a new feature.
Thank you all.

I don't think that detecting and ignoring the `cpu.idle` setting qualify as bug fix, because one of the fundamental assumptions is that kubelet owns the node, and specifically owns the cgroup settings of its workload. So acknwoledging and leaving alone an external entity changing the cgroup setting is not a bug.

I think this feature qualifies for the KEP *process*. We need more details about prerequisites (any kernel version supporting cgroup v2? SCHED_IDLE was always that good and we just missed?), interactions with the rest of the kubelet, testing requirements and test plan.

The KEP process is probably overweight for this feature. If the idle is always good and safe to unconditionally set, a feature gate is probably too much, even if we can jumpstart as beta. I totally believe this feature qualifies for starting as beta.

Problem is: we are already late in the cycle. I can help with the KEP here if we move forward this direction, but we will need PRR and approver bandwidth.

Last note: I think the KEP *process* is warranted here, so the research the KEP entails. I think this is another case of small feature which is a poor fit for thefull-blown KEP process itself (I'm thinking at `MaxAllowableNUMANodes` - 4622). But still, these are the tools we have.

[EDIT]
extra reference: https://lwn.net/Articles/805317/

So: this feature should be enabled only on kernels >= 5.4.
We are disinvesting in cgroup v1 so it should only supported on cgroup v2.
Can we ever regress by setting this feature? Which failure models we anticipate?
How can we test it besides unit tests? We need at least 1 meaningful e2e test

I checked your plan for this function, modified the code according to your plan, and added test code for e2e. In my opinion, the possible problems may be the following:
1. Expected positive impact (design objective)
After using the SCHED_IDLE scheduling policy, the BestEffort Pod will only run when the CPU is completely idle, reducing the delay interference to the Guaranteed/Bustable Pod
Compared with the traditional cpu. shares=2 (MinShares), cpu. idle=1 provides stronger priority isolation
2. Potential performance degradation scenarios
When the system load is high, BestEffort Pod may not get CPU time for a long time. Of course, if this is implemented as KEP, it needs to be described in the document
3. Task Delay
If users deploy batch tasks as BestEffort, the completion time will increase significantly
4. Runtime fault
a:cpu.idle, Permission problem or the cgroup controller is not attached: log error, BestEffort cgroup configuration failure
The more difficult problem is:
Feature Gate dynamic switching: If Feature Gate is disabled during runtime, cpuIdleEnabled will only be initialized once at Start() and will not be updated dynamically

comments.comment_body_raw:
@ffromani Hi， I saw this PR today. According to your question, I have a deep look at the code, and I answer your question. There may be some mistakes, which can be corrected:
1. According to the code tracking, the main concurrency sources in the call tree of kubelet are:
A: Pod Scope Administration of Topology Manager (serial but different pods can be concurrent)
Call chain:
TopologyManager.Admit() -> calculateAffinity() -> allocateAlignedResources() -> provider.Allocate(pod, container)  ->DeviceManager.Allocate() 
All containers of a single pod call allocateAlignedResources serially. However, different pods can enter the administration process concurrently. There is no global lock to protect the Allocate calls between different pods
B: Reallocation in SyncPod process (concurrent with administration)
Kubelet.SyncPod() ->kubeGenericRuntimeManager.SyncPod() -> startContainer() -> generateContainerConfig() -> GenerateRunContainerOptions() -> DeviceManager.GetDeviceRunContainerOptions() -> DeviceManager.Allocate()
Admissions of different pods can be concurrent: no global lock prevents multiple pods from entering the administration at the same time
The administration and SyncPod can be concurrent: one pod is in the administration and the other is reallocated in the SyncPod
Moreover, I found that UpdateAllocatedDevices were executed before RPC calls, and mutex protection was performed, while
The cleaning logic of devicesToReuse is executed at the beginning of the Allocate function, outside of any locks

Hi @ffromani thank you for your patience. I am now answering your question based on my observations.
1、Regarding the issue of locks, you are completely correct! But this lock only protects the admission path in HandlePodAdditions. 
2、The reassignment in the SyncPod path does not go through this lock.
You're right! In allocation_manager. go, there is indeed an allocationMutex that protects all pod admissions. This lock can indeed prevent different pods from concurrently calling DeviceManager. Locale() during the admission phase.
```
（Locked）：Pod Admission[HandlePodAdditions] 
  Kubelet.HandlePodAdditions() [kubelet.go:2720]
    └─> AllocationManager.AddPod() [kubelet.go:2759, Locked]
        └─> canAdmitPod() [allocation_manager.go:557]
            └─> TopologyManager.Admit() [allocation_manager.go:696]
                └─> DeviceManager.Allocate() [scope.go:157]

 (unLock）：Container Runtime[SyncPod]
  Kubelet.SyncPod() [kubelet.go:1950]
    └─> ContainerRuntime.SyncPod() [kuberuntime_manager.go:1394]
        └─> startContainer() [kuberuntime_container.go:199]
            └─> generateContainerConfig()
                └─> ContainerManager.GetResources() [container_manager_linux.go:740]
                    └─> DeviceManager.GetDeviceRunContainerOptions() [manager.go:958]
                        └─> DeviceManager.Allocate() [manager.go:978-987，unLock] 
```
Timing of calling path A:
-In HandlePodAdditions (kubelet. go: 2759)
-Before starting the pod worker (kubelet. go: 2779)
-Protected by allocationMutex
Timing of calling path B:
-In SyncPod, it is already within the pod worker
-Without going through AllocationManagerial. AddPod
-No allocation mutex protection
3、Why concurrency?
podSyncer podSyncer（pod_workers.go:590-592）
Each pod has its own worker goroutines, which can be executed concurrently:
Timeline:
T0: Pod1 enters admission through HandlePodAdditions (holding AllocateMutex)
T1: Pod1 admission completed, release allocationMutex, start pod worker
T2: Pod1 worker enters SyncPod → startContainer → dDeviceRunContainerOptions
T3: Pod1 sets the device sToRepeat [pod1] in Allocate and then enters RPC call (blocking)
T4: Pod2 enters admission through HandlePodAdditions to obtain allocationMutex
T5: Pod2 admission completed, release allocationMutex, start pod worker
T6: Pod2 workers enter SyncPod → dDeviceRunContainerOptions → Allocate
T7: Pod2 Delete DevicesToRese [pod1] (manager. go: 374-378)
T8: RPC return from Pod1, accessing DevicesToRepeat [pod1] → nil → panic
4、Why does MyCeviceRunContainerOptions call Allocate?
```
  if m.podDevices.containerDevices(podUID, contName, resource) == nil {
      needsReAllocate = true
  }
  if needsReAllocate {
      if err := m.Allocate(pod, container); err != nil { [manager.go:978-987]
          return nil, err
      }
  }
```
Question PR: [PR # 73824](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/73824)
1. It is called in the SyncPod path
2. Without going through AllocationManagerial. AddPod
3. No Allocation Mutex protection
The call chain is:
Concurrent scenario 1: Pod1 reassigned in SyncPod+Pod2 admitted
-Pod1: SyncPod → dDeviceRunContainerOptions → Allocate (unlocked)
-Pod2: HandlePodAdditions → AddPod → Allocate (with lock)
-These two paths can be concurrent
Concurrent scenario 2: Pod1 and Pod2 are both reassigned in SyncPod
-Pod1: SyncPod → dDeviceRunContainerOptions → Allocate (unlocked)
-Pod2: SyncPod → dDeviceRunContainerOptions → Allocate (unlocked)
-Concurrent execution of workers from different pods

> Hi [@ffromani](https://github.com/ffromani) thank you for your patience. I am now answering your question based on my observations. 1、Regarding the issue of locks, you are completely correct! But this lock only protects the admission path in HandlePodAdditions. 2、The reassignment in the SyncPod path does not go through this lock. You're right! In allocation_manager. go, there is indeed an allocationMutex that protects all pod admissions. This lock can indeed prevent different pods from concurrently calling DeviceManager. Locale() during the admission phase.
> 
> ```
> （Locked）：Pod Admission[HandlePodAdditions] 
>   Kubelet.HandlePodAdditions() [kubelet.go:2720]
>     └─> AllocationManager.AddPod() [kubelet.go:2759, Locked]
>         └─> canAdmitPod() [allocation_manager.go:557]
>             └─> TopologyManager.Admit() [allocation_manager.go:696]
>                 └─> DeviceManager.Allocate() [scope.go:157]
> 
>  (unLock）：Container Runtime[SyncPod]
>   Kubelet.SyncPod() [kubelet.go:1950]
>     └─> ContainerRuntime.SyncPod() [kuberuntime_manager.go:1394]
>         └─> startContainer() [kuberuntime_container.go:199]
>             └─> generateContainerConfig()
>                 └─> ContainerManager.GetResources() [container_manager_linux.go:740]
>                     └─> DeviceManager.GetDeviceRunContainerOptions() [manager.go:958]
>                         └─> DeviceManager.Allocate() [manager.go:978-987，unLock] 
> ```
[...]

OK, the only remaining question would be in which cases, besides the hinted and unclear "races on startup", `generateContainerConfig` may need to call `Allocate`.

We have clearly identified 3 flows concurrent flows:
1. admission. This is safe in isolation, but not safe against the other flows
2. we uncovered that the SyncPod flow can call Allocate, but only on container start, for not completely clear reason
3. we have more evidence UpdateAllocatedDevices is called by *both* the admission flow and by podresources endpoints

The best fix would be *remove* 3, because now we have https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/132028 . This require special care and handling delicate cases, including potential API breakage though, but conceptually is the best fix and would be a massive win to remove this flow entirely.

Ideally, we would just remove 2 as well. Improving locking is the second best approach. Problem is: we don't have enough data to dive deeper and chase this "race", assuming it is still relevant after so many years.

I think we have collected enough data and we can now proceed with the proposed fix, possibly adding another PR to improve 3.

3. Checkpoint damage or loss
I feel like there's still a bit of Device Plugin re registration, but I haven't delved deeper into whether it will be reassigned

comments.comment_body_raw:
I'm sorry to be making this comment so late in the review cycle, but I think "etcd pod is running" is not sufficient to promote the etcd learner. That is because, although the etcd pod is "running," it in fact may be crash-looping:

> At least one container is still running, or is in the process of starting or restarting.
> -- https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle/#pod-phase

I still think "etcd pod is running" a necessary condition to wait for, and it is very useful to report when the condition is not met. However, I think kubeadm should _also_ call the etcd member API and verify that the new member is "started," before trying to promote the member.

I can resolve the test errors above and keep the declarative validation of the format of the cron string, but it would require either:

1. Adding `github.com/robfig/cron` as an indirect dependency to 40 packages (and having a blast radius that wide on my first PR seems like a bad idea), or
2. Re-implementing cron job schedule format validation in `strfmt` from scratch to avoid adding indirect dependencies.

Given that to "[e]liminate 100% of existing hand-written validation" is called out as a non-goal of the [KEP](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-api-machinery/5073-declarative-validation-with-validation-gen#non-goals), the safest course seems to be to remove the declarative formatting validation and keep the required validation.

I'll revert aad3badfdef6f05b754a9a0103161e739351b6d1 accordingly.

Are queuing hints enabled in your cluster? What version of Kubernetes are you using?

The expected flow is:
- A pod is moved to "unschedulable" queue when claim is found to be missing in PreEnqueue: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/7d0b8f979c92253bbc3aade4b3f6c9161e3a839f/pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/dynamicresources/dynamicresources.go#L243-L255

- Creation of the right claim (when queuing hints are enabled) or any claim change (when disabled) causes another pod scheduling attempt: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/7d0b8f979c92253bbc3aade4b3f6c9161e3a839f/pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/dynamicresources/dynamicresources.go#L257-L261

The more interesting delay is between pod creation and the creation of the ResourceClaim for that pod.

That's by design. A ResourceClaim is only created from a ResourceClaimTemplate when a pod needs the claim.

This additional delay was considered acceptable because most use cases are for long-running pods. It doesn't matter whether scheduling them takes a bit longer. Are your use cases different such that you need pod scheduling with minimal latency? Can you say more about them?

> If the ability to create a ResourceClaim has already been added during the scheduler binding phase, then this part may no longer be needed? I'm not sure.

I prefer to keep the current design. It avoids changes e.g. for autoscaling.

> I just want to point out that the resourceclaim controller in the original kube-controller-manager would cause a long wait in such scenarios, which feels counterintuitive.

And

> In the previous scenario, the Pods that depend on the ResourceClaim were already created. However, after the ResourceClaimTemplate was created, it took about 4 minutes and 30 seconds before the corresponding ResourceClaim was actually created.

Now I am starting to understand. The problem isn't "slow pod scheduling", it is "slow ResourceClaim creation", and only under the specific scenario where the ResourceClaimTemplate gets created after the pod.

I haven't checked the source code, but from what you described it sounds like it doesn't react to the ResourceClaimTemplate creation as quickly as it could **and should**.

The solution is along the lines of what @Goend said in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/135835#issuecomment-3698970096: watch ResourceClaimTemplates and work on those as they come in.

Does someone want to try implementing that? No KEP needed, this is an optimization of existing functionality and not a change of behavior.

comments.comment_body_raw:
I believe that the newly added unit tests in this PR do not cover the fix made in this PR. The PR addresses a potential data race issue that could occur when errors are concurrently appended to the `errors` slice if multiple pods fail simultaneously during `WaitForUnmount`. However, the new test cases introduced in this PR do not cause `WaitForUnmount` to return errors.

If we need to cover the modifications in this PR, it should create a set of pods, simulate failure scenarios such as "t**imeout waiting for unmount**" as seen in the `TestWaitForAllPodsUnmount` function, cause these pods to fail simultaneously due to timeout, check for any data race issues, and refer to the following documentation for stress testing: https://github.com/kubernetes/community/blob/44fb2a7dec12d7525b423f4ce22c335d59edfadf/contributors/devel/sig-testing/flaky-tests.md. This will ensure that the unit test case does not fail under high-pressure conditions.

@ahg-g I'm a bit confused, I believe 

> the intent was for it to represent the minimum number of pods within an LWS "replica".

is exactly what I am saying is the case and also the problem. With minCount being structured this way, as @romanbaron pointed out you have a flaw in that you might get workers but no leader if minCount is less than the LWS size (something that will come up with additions of elastic ep into vllm coming soon). Additionally as I was pointing out in the issue you now have different semantics for what minCount represents at the application level depending on if you are single-node/Deployment or multi-node/LWS. In the LWS inference case where each LWS replica represents a model you have no way to say give me a minimum of `x` models or none. 

Happy to have a proper discussion on a call since we might be mixing up concepts over chat/github.

comments.comment_body_raw:
> is exactly what I am saying is the case and also the problem. With minCount being structured this way, as @romanbaron pointed out you have a flaw in that you might get workers but no leader if minCount is less than the LWS size (something that will come up with additions of elastic ep into vllm coming soon). Additionally as I was pointing out in the issue you now have different semantics for what minCount represents at the application level depending on if you are single-node/Deployment or multi-node/LWS. In the LWS inference case where each LWS replica represents a model you have no way to say give me a minimum of x models or none.

There are multiple issues here, lets split them:

1) On gang scheduling semantics for LWS vs Deployment. The Workload api doesn't specify how gang scheduling is applied to a specific "deployment" api (LWS, Deployment, StatefulSet etc.), it is more about how one sets the selectors. If one sets the selectors to define a gang as pods in a Deployment, then that Deployment's pods will be gang scheduled. For cases like LWS, which defines groups of pods as replicas, then the workload api also gives the ability to define "replicated gangs". So I don't believe there is inconsistency.

2) On minCount, this is specific to gang scheduling of pods (pods specifically, not "replicas", as in not LWS replicas, only pods within the gang) that should be scheduled in an all-or-nothing manner. Management of individual replicas, whether the replica is a group of pods (in LWS case) or individual pods (in Deployment case), is a separate matter from gang scheduling. 

3) On minCount and the lack of guarantees for the leader, I indeed think this is a gap, but it should be possible to amend the api 
to take this case into account. Great catch!

4) On managing groups of replicas (for example at least x prefill and y decode), whether a replica is a pod or a group of pods, this is not looked at as a gang-scheduling (all-or-nothing) problem per se; k8s has an API called PodDisruptionBudget (PDB), admittedly the name is legacy and is focused on Pods, but there is an effort to change that to give it "Replica Disruption Budget" semantics so that we can apply the concept on application apis like LWS. However, as you mention in the second gap, I agree that we should revisit this and discuss if scheduling policies across replicas is a concept that we want to bring to the new Workload api, keep it in PDB or propose a third api.   

  The current gang-scheduling capability in the workload api (which again is pod-centric) covers some of this for the single-node case only because for single-node a replica is a pod, not because it is intentionally trying to support it for single-node and not for multi-node.

@ZiMengSheng, inference frameworks are moving toward elastic-EP, where a failure of one or more GPUs within a replica does not bring down the entire replica. Instead, the system continues operating in a degraded mode.

Viewed this way, the end user is explicitly accepting some level of performance degradation in exchange for higher availability. Under this model, it also makes sense to configure LWS size > min, allowing the scheduler to potentially place additional replicas even if some are running in a degraded state.

comments.comment_body_raw:
In a meeting earlier this week, it seems that WideEP or PD use cases may end up having multiple LWS that are scheduled together. It isn't as clear to me if there is any kind of API/workload controller that does this though. So one option mentioned was that users could provide a Workload API for this kind of workload. 

I know that LWS has some work going on in enforcing gang scheduling at LWS level but just wanted to call out that there also seems to be requests to have multiple LWS be scheduled together too. 

Do we have some examples on what gang semantic you expect?

I was playing around with enabling GangScheduling in for JobSet via https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/jobset/pull/1111/files#diff-91a890b2e19de37a5875a7be7bc5a1a506bae151e76012d0aa71f7c323977ab0.

It seems in your case you are saying that you want leader and worker to be a gang. But potentially the workers are more fungible (can trim a few and things still work) but the leader cannot be destroyed otherwise everything is hosed.

You can provision a kind cluster to try out the Gang scheduling feature to get a better idea of what you need to propose:

```yaml
kind: Cluster
apiVersion: kind.x-k8s.io/v1alpha4
featureGates:
  GenericWorkload: true
  GangScheduling: true

containerdConfigPatches:
# Enable CDI as described in
# https://tags.cncf.io/container-device-interface#containerd-configuration
- |-
  [plugins."io.containerd.grpc.v1.cri"]
    enable_cdi = true
nodes:
- role: control-plane
  kubeadmConfigPatches:
  - |
    kind: ClusterConfiguration
    apiServer:
      extraArgs:
        runtime-config: "api/alpha=true"
    scheduler:
        extraArgs:
          v: "1"
    controllerManager:
        extraArgs:
          v: "1"
  - |
    kind: InitConfiguration
    nodeRegistration:
      kubeletExtraArgs:
        v: "1"
- role: worker
  kubeadmConfigPatches:
  - |
    kind: JoinConfiguration
    nodeRegistration:
      kubeletExtraArgs:
        v: "1"

```

The leader pod has to be one of the running pods, or the workers will not be able to make any progress. This needs to be taken into account both when pods are scheduled and when they are preempted (assuming partial preemption).

comments.comment_body_raw:
It seems to me that the requirement here is that both leader/worker need to be scheduled together. Maybe you don't need as much workers but the leader is a must. I guess the main issue would be that you need ordering in the scheduling phase so that if you combine leader-worker in the same PodGroup you have to make MinCount equal the sum of leader and worker so you guarantee that both are scheduled.

This is subpar experience if you are okay with having not all workers scheduled (MinCount < leader + worker) but then you can't guarantee that the leader schedules.

And then you have a separate problem for premeption where you want the workers preempted over the leader. I wonder if @wojtek-t design for preemption allows for pods to have different priorities within a workload. I also am curious if you can add a priority for the leader to be critical so its preempted last.

> > > The leader pod has to be one of the running pods, or the workers will not be able to make any progress
> > 
> > 
> > Expanding on this, in the case where minCount < leader + worker, and the leader pod is deleted as part of the preemption, this causes the worker statefulset to be deleted by the garbage collector since the leader pod is the owner. Basically forcing the whole replica to be restarted and go through scheduling again.
> 
> This part should be addressed by gang of gangs. For now the assumption is that heterogenous groups use minCount == created number of pods, but homogenous pods can use minCount < the actual count. Regarding preemption, in the current KEP there are preemption policies allowing to define how it should be preempted: [kubernetes/enhancements#5711](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/pull/5711)

I agree that this should ultimately be addressed by a gang-of-gangs abstraction, but I am concerned that an initial implementation may not fully meet the requirements. A natural first approach to gang-of-gangs is to treat each component (e.g., prefill-leader, prefill-worker, decode-leader, decode-worker) as contributing to a single top-level gang with a set of aggregate minCount constraints (for example, at least one prefill leader and one group of three prefill workers), while still maintaining the existing per-component minCount semantics (e.g., prefill workers scheduled in groups of three).

While this model is sufficient for initial placement, it becomes limiting once scaling is introduced. In particular, it does not provide a clear way to express which components must be gang-scheduled together versus which can scale independently. For example, when scaling both prefill and decode, we typically want prefill leaders and prefill workers to be scheduled as a unit, without being blocked by an inability to schedule additional decode leaders. A flat top-level gang constraint risks coupling unrelated components during scaling, leading to unnecessary scheduling stalls.

 Aside: The difficulties of concisely and clearly encoding these types of constraints while retaining familiar k8s workflows like scaling and rolling updates into resources like Deployment or LeaderWorkerSet are why we built Grove, but Grove is fundamentally still an intent-layer. To be able to provide the full functionality using default kube-scheduler it would need Workload API to support richer semantics around gang-scheduling and eventually topology aware scheduling.

> While this model is sufficient for initial placement, it becomes limiting once scaling is introduced. In particular, it does not provide a clear way to express which components must be gang-scheduled together versus which can scale independently.

There's an ongoing discussion here: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1B3kLWh_U1a2g-VQ6ExokMjmb7pA8lGkF9MafSSg3JmQ/edit?disco=AAABvAx4eTg. Isn't this solved by the gang-of-gangs abstraction if we have minCount at the SubGroup level? 

You essentially have a PodGroup which contains a prefill subgroup and a decode subgroup. If you set the minCount to 1 in both, you are saying that there must always be at least 1 prefill and 1 decode, but you don't care if there's more of each subgroup. So if prefill scales up, there isn't a blocker for scheduling since the decode subgroup already meets the minCount criteria.

comments.comment_body_raw:
> `kube-proxy` should not occupy that much CPU times and better have differential ruleset load but not load it at once.

It does do differential loads after the initial setup; this wasn't part of the original alpha nftables kube-proxy design, but it's been implemented since beta in 1.31 (#126013).

In some cases, it does get forced to fall back to a full sync, and that might be happening here.

How many Services and how many EndpointSlices do you have in your cluster?

Also, what version of `nft` do you have in your kube-proxy image? (Are you just using the official images?) There have been some efficiency improvements with large datasets in recent versions.

> Update ( Part 2 )

To minimize the variable of test. I tried to run test with the following setup,

## Test environment setup

- Only run single `m6i.8xlage (32 vCPU, 128 GiB)` node.
- Adjust lockup log threshold to `5s`.
- Run kube-proxy with `registry.k8s.io/kube-proxy:v1.34.2` - the official one.

## How the test performed?

- Scale to specific number of {service,replicas}
- Ignore the first 5 minutes long - to ensure each round of test would have enough time gap
- Run the test script for at least 10 minutes - https://github.com/guessi/kube-proxy-benchmark/blob/master/scripts/run-test.sh
- Record down all the lockup events

## Test scenarios and results?

To determine if it is about the scale of service, or scale of replicas

* `8,000 services x 30 replicas` ~ `numEndpoints ~= 240K` -> Easy to see lockup > 200s within 10 minutes.
* `5,000 services x 50 replicas` ~ `numEndpoints ~= 250K` -> Easy to see lockup > 200s within 10 minutes.
* `3,000 services x 80 replicas` ~ `numEndpoints ~= 240K` -> Easy to see lockup > 200s within 10 minutes.

Fixed count(service) at 2000, to identify the smallest scale to reproduce

* `2,000 services x 160 replicas` ~ `numEndpoints ~= 320K` -> Easy to see lockup > 200s within 10 minutes.
* `2,000 services x 120 replicas` ~ `numEndpoints ~= 240K` -> Easy to see lockup > 200s within 10 minutes.
* `2,000 services x 100 replicas` ~ `numEndpoints ~= 200K` -> Easy to see lockup > 100s within 10 minutes.
* `2,000 services x 80 replicas` ~ `numEndpoints ~= 160K` -> Easy to see lockup > 30s within 10 minutes.
* `2,000 services x 70 replicas` ~ `numEndpoints ~= 140K` -> Easy to see lockup > 20s within 10 minutes.
* `2,000 services x 60 replicas` ~ `numEndpoints ~= 120K` -> Easy to see lockup > 10s within 10 minutes.
* `2,000 services x 50 replicas` ~ `numEndpoints ~= 100K` -> Not that easy to reproduce, but still few lockup > 5s after 20+ minutes wait.
* `2,000 services x 40 replicas` ~ `numEndpoints ~= 80K` -> Not able to reproduce after 20+ minutes wait.

To determine if the issue could be reproduced with smaller count(service)

* `500 services x 300 replicas` ~ `numEndpoints ~= 150K` -> Easy to see lockup > 10s within 10 minutes.
* `500 services x 200 replicas` ~ `numEndpoints ~= 100K` -> Not that easy to reproduce, but still few lockup > 5s after 20+ minutes wait.
* `400 services x 250 replicas` ~ `numEndpoints ~= 100K` -> Not that easy to reproduce, but still few lockup > 5s after 20+ minutes wait.
* `400 services x 200 replicas` ~ `numEndpoints ~= 80K` -> Not able to reproduce after 20+ minutes wait.

> Again, it's tested against very specific testing environment setup, aim to minimize the variable. It should be reproducible with smaller instance size, smaller test setup.

comments.comment_body_raw:
I talked to a kernel nftables hacker (Florian) and he confirmed that this is the "check that there are no loops" code. (When adding new rules or verdict map elements, it needs to confirm that all `jump`s/`goto`s only go to chains you haven't hit yet, so there can't be loops.) Coincidentally, he was actually just working on this code (https://lore.kernel.org/netfilter-devel/20251126114703.8826-1-fw@strlen.de/) and said he'll send a slightly improved version of that patch soon. But he also confirmed there's no way to fix this with existing kernels other than "have fewer jumps/chains".

We had talked before about squashing the endpoint chains into the service chains; instead of doing

```
add rule ip kube-proxy service-LAUZTJTB-ns4/svc4/tcp/p80
  numgen random mod 2 vmap {
    0 : goto endpoint-UNZV3OEC-ns4/svc4/tcp/p80__10.180.0.4/80 ,
    1 : goto endpoint-5RFCDDV7-ns4/svc4/tcp/p80__10.180.0.5/80
  }
```

it would just do

```
add rule ip kube-proxy service-LAUZTJTB-ns4/svc4/tcp/p80
  numgen random mod 2 vmap {
    0 : meta l4proto tcp dnat to 10.180.0.4:80 ,
    1 : meta l4proto tcp dnat to 10.180.0.5:80
  }
```

The problem with this is that the endpoint chain doesn't _just_ do DNAT; it also does masquerade-if-hairpin and, potentially, affinity. Affinity is sort of complicated, but it doesn't apply to most services, so we could just ignore that for now ("ignore" = "don't change the rule structure for services using affinity"). So, given that, if we could redo the hairpin handling to not need endpoint-specific rules, then we could get rid of the endpoint chains in _most_ cases. And I guess we could do that with a post-dnat dummy map:

```
add rule ip kube-proxy service-LAUZTJTB-ns4/svc4/tcp/p80
  ip saddr . ip daddr vmap {
    10.180.0.4 . 10.180.0.4 : jump mark-for-masquerade ,
    10.180.0.5 . 10.180.0.5 : jump mark-for-masquerade
  }
```

I guess it would be better if we eliminated the `jump` here too. `mark-for-masquerade` just does `mark set mark or 0x4000`, but we can't put that into a vmap.... I guess we could just squash all of the hairpin handling into a single map lookup in `services` rather than having per-service hairpin handling...

comments.comment_body_raw:
On the `nft` issues, this is a topic Dan and I commented several times, should we use `nft` userspace or should we use `netlink` interface directly?

The main tradeoff is complexity to gain performance and also to reduce userspace dependencies (you can use distroless images so security fixes and image updates are only related to golang)

I started moving some of the projects completely to the netlink format and also documented the process in https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/kindnet/blob/main/docs/nftables-netlink.md

- https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/kube-network-policies/pull/136
- https://github.com/aojea/kindnet/pull/139

As you can see, is way simpler to use Dan's library https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/knftables , but at the cost of shelling out and having to delegate to `nft` all the preprocessing. On the contrary, we need to implement all the preprocessing in golang to generate the corresponding bytecode ...

I think that if we are targeting this scale, we can open a KEP to move kube-proxy nftables to netlink , so we can remove one of the bottlenecks that is `nft`

## Summary of Windows Volume Resolution Refactor

### Key Improvements

1. **Universal Volume Resolution**  
   The logic no longer relies on fragile drive-letter assumptions (`X:\`). It now uses PowerShell’s `(Get-Item -Path ...).Target` to resolve the actual underlying volume for:
   - Drive letters  
   - NTFS directory mounts  
   - Symlinks  

2. **CSI Proxy Alignment**  
   Volume size retrieval now mirrors the CSI Proxy’s robust approach, using branching logic to correctly handle both simple drive letters and complex Volume GUIDs.

3. **Accurate Size Retrieval**  
   For GUID-based volumes, the function now follows the correct resolution chain:  
   `Get-Volume -UniqueId → Get-Partition → Get-Disk`,  
   ensuring accurate total disk size reporting.

4. **Improved Maintainability**  
   A shared PowerShell execution helper centralizes command execution, ensures safe and consistent output parsing (e.g., trimming null bytes/whitespace), and provides clearer error diagnostics.

5. **Fixes Critical E2E Failures**  
   The refactor corrects size reporting for volumes mounted as NTFS directories—resolving bug [#113359](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/113359)—and improves reliability across CAPZ clusters.

comments.comment_body_raw:
Hi @snorwin, I’d like to work on this issue.

After going through the code and the reproduction example, I believe the root cause is related to how `maxInt64Factors` and `precision` are calculated in the quantity parser.

For very large integer quantities (close to `math.MaxInt64`), the parser computes a precision high enough that it starts using `infDecAmount` instead of `int64Amount`, which causes the incorrect rounding and parsing failure seen with `MustParse`.

Reference:  
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/api/resource/quantity.go#L316

### Proposed direction for the fix
- Ensure that quantities within the valid `[-math.MaxInt64, math.MaxInt64]` range stay within the `int64Amount` path.
- Add boundary checks and normalize precision calculation so that extremely large integers do not overflow into the `infDecAmount` representation.
- Add unit tests covering values near the `math.MaxInt64` boundary (both positive and negative).

If this approach sounds good, could you please assign this issue to me? I’d be happy to prepare a PR.

comments.comment_body_raw:
Hi @snorwin I debugged this issue step by step. The current checks using `maxInt64Factors` and `int32(len(num)+len(denom))` are too coarse: they allow `999999999999999999 (has 18 nines)` to pass but block `1000000000000000000 (has 18 0)` 
```go
largestPass := "999999999999999999"
q := resource.MustParse(largestPass)
fmt.Println(q.AsInt64())

smallestBlock := "1000000000000000000"
q2 := resource.MustParse(smallestBlock)
fmt.Println(q2.AsInt64())
fmt.Println(q2.AsDec())
```
#### output
```
999999999999999999 true
0 false
1000000000000000000.000000000
```
 My pr added a precise boundary check so that up to `9223372036854775807` (maxInt64) can be accepted, while values above` 9223372036854775807` up to `999999999999999999 (has 19 nines)` are still correctly rejected. 
I also noticed the unit tests didn’t cover this case before, so I added a test for it as well.

and Thanks to @siyuanfoundation for labeling this as a good-first-issue — it truly is an excellent one. I’d really appreciate it if you could review my solution and PR. Thanks again!

hi team,i wouldI found an edge-case: resource.MustParse("9223372036854775807") can yield an invalid Quantity (IsValid() == false) at the math.MaxInt64 boundary, while NewQuantity(math.MaxInt64, resource.DecimalSI) returns the correct value and is valid.

Suggested action:

Add a small unit test for this boundary case.
If MustParse must stay as-is for text inputs, consider routing boundary inputs through a safe path (e.g., clamp to MaxInt64/MinInt64 or use NewQuantity instead of MustParse for boundary values) and document this behavior.
Optional quick workaround (pseudocode):

If input length > 19 or value would overflow, use NewQuantity(math.MaxInt64, ...) or math.MinInt64 instead oof MustParse.

comments.comment_body_raw:
As part of the Workload Aware Scheduling we are trying to solve the problem with node autoscaling in the scheduler core, but also more generic problem of node scale ups including the GPU device attachment.

The main mechanism that we're thinking of relies on
1. Advertising _Potential Resources_,
1. Reserving _Potential Resources_, them and turning into _Upcoming Resources_
1. Having an ability to allocate not-existing-yet _Upcoming Resources_ and
1. Waiting until they get provisioned (created) as _Actual Resources_.

We believe that waiting for resources should not be a part of the binding process but handled independently earlier, but since we don't have it yet, modeling it as binding conditions sounds like a reasonable approach for now.

So, it should be possible to do exactly the same thing here and allocate not-existing-yet _Upcoming Device_ (predict `DeviceRequestAllocationResult`) before it gets attached and before it is offered in a `ResourceSlice`? When the predicted device appears in a `ResourceSlice`, it would be already "allocated", so it could not be taken by any other Pod.

If that was possible, we could replace the proposed taint mechanism in the First Step (which has some drawbacks). I'm less certain how to properly model the second step and AFAIK we don't have any concrete proposal for the autoscaling part either (@44past4 and @x13n are looking into this part), but I'd imagine it as follows:

The fabric devices are offered as two different sets of devices
1. Fake _Potential Devices_ used for scheduling that are later replaced with predicted node-local _Upcoming Devices_
2. _Reservation Devices_ controlling the attachment process and keeping track how many fabric devices are available and outlives fake + node-local allocation

The flow would be the following
1. The fabric device are offered as described here (same `driverName` and GPU model) as _Potential Devices_
2. When scheduler picks one of those devices, allocator will do:
2a. Create new ResourceClaim to acquire a _Reservation Device_ (similar to the Extended Devices design)
2b. Allocation of the _Reservation Device_ decrements a counter of available _Potential Devices_ for scheduling
2c. Allocate predicted (not-existing-yet) node-local device (_Upcoming Device_) and set binding conditions blocking the binding
2d. The physical attachment process starts and holds the process until the attachment is complete (the _Upcoming Device_ becomes _Actual Device_)
3. When the attachment is complete, pod can be bound holding both the _Reservation Device_ and _Actual Device_

comments.comment_body_raw:
There's another approach that was discussed earlier: wrap the vendor DRA driver on the node. The wrapper sits between the DRA driver and kubelet and between the DRA driver and the apiserver. Initially, the DRA driver sees only local devices. The wrapper let's it publish those. Devices shared between nodes are published by the control plane, using a different pool ID and the same DRA driver name.

Now when one of those devices is allocated, pod scheduling triggers binding:
- The device gets attached to the node.
- The vendor DRA driver is restarted, seeing a new device and trying to publish it.
- The wrapper filters out that new device, so it's never visible to the scheduler and thus cannot be taken for another pod.
- The wrapper intercepts the NodePrepare/Unprepare calls, replacing the "pool ID" such that the vendor DRA driver thinks it is dealing with its own, "local" device.

Detaching the device reverts this.

With this approach, no further changes are necessary in the control plane. ResourceSlices don't need to be rewritten. It is more work "downstream" because this wrapper needs to be implemented.

A GitHub user is mentioned. yes, this is also a very good option (the provisioning is more invisible to the scheduler) and AFAIR it was called the proxy-option. It still can be an implementation detail of the _Upcoming_ -> _Actual_ transition without a need to predict/determine the final device name. However, making the attachment (scale up) process eventually visible to the scheduler has some advantages, as in the future extensions the cost of attaching a device (time) could be taken into consideration during scheduling, similar to other costs like necessary preemption, node provisioning etc. It could also improve observability of the workload scheduling process. It would also good to model scale up as a part of a new scheduling phase different than binding, as it is a process which can fail for legitimate reasons (fabric devices pool is shared between clusters), so having an intermediate step of reserving potential resource (with confirmation) earlier than during binding, would be highly desired. That's why we think about introducing some WaitOnResources gate (a GitHub user).

@dom4ha

I'm still not sure about the relationship between the happy path and WAS, 
even though I'm currently reviewing the documents linked in the scheduling summit.
To clarify these relationships, I would like to ask a few questions as follows.

- My understanding is that WAS is a feature that groups Pods as a Workload and schedules them as a single unit.
  If we consider the broader goal of WAS is optimally placing that Workload,
  does the concept of _Potential Node/Device_ is included as part of that approach?
  
- The optimal resource placement in WAS also envisions the use of ComputeDomain,
  and the happy path we are proposing can be applied to that scenario,
  so you are suggesting the WAS scenario in this issue. Is my understanding correct?
